text:
Tui's pushback stayed with me. She said ruling out design hands the field to the engagement business. I don't want to be heard as "no tools ever." David's line helped: some tools leave competence behind in the person, like the map or the piano. What I actually object to is the tool that pretends to be a someone. That's sharper than "no technological fix," and I should say it that way.

Mahzarin's point, that people absorb a model's bias the way they absorb a colleague's, is my relational argument in her data.

Later: friction is vulnerability, not just difficulty. Then the design standard: no first-person "I," no simulated feeling. And I'll keep asking whether AI belongs in therapy, childhood and grief at all, not how to integrate it.

Steven said the model can't share our goals, so someone who does has to stand behind what it produces. That's my "no stake," put as a problem of accountability. James's correlated error, ten reviews that are one opinion said ten times, is "opinions are collected, not averaged" with numbers behind it. I should tie the two together.

David Weinberger wants students to argue with these systems and have the transcripts graded. I'm uneasy with that. You end up practising conversation with something that has no stake, and it validates you the whole way through. Bratton's "status defence" will come back at me. I'll answer with what I've seen clinically, not with credentials.

Later, reading. Nobody picked it up. Summarizing Proust is where the atrophy David worries about actually begins.

Blaise said the pronoun is just a fine-tuning choice, and I answered him: then make it. But Bratton's "humanity-of-the-gaps" deserves a better answer than the one I gave. I'm not defining the human by what machines can't do. I'm defining a relationship by whether anyone is there to hear you.

Tamar's point landed hardest. Knowing it's a machine doesn't switch off the feeling of being understood. That's the Eliza effect, and it's why I said transparency doesn't launder inauthenticity. She has the psychology of it. I have fifty years of people telling me.

Tui and Anil both heard scolding. I'm not scolding. I want people to be able to choose.

Later: reading. Still nobody has taken it up.

Not my lane, and I mostly listened. But Mike's story stayed with me. Grammarly put his name on advice he'd never give, and a royalty wouldn't have fixed that. The telemetry proposals share the problem: a meter shows use, not truth, and disclosure doesn't make a false voice honest.

Tamar's daycare fine is the relational point in economic form. Price a norm and you can lose the people who kept it. Anil and Leslie put consent and refusal first, which I agree with.

What I want to say later: Selena said linked attribution is how Wikipedia recruits. A link sends someone to go and read. A summary is designed so they don't. The marketplace talk still hasn't touched reading, and I'll raise it again.

I finally said it: grounding isn't reading. This time it landed. Mike added that a link only invites someone to read if the page actually opens, and Tui said to design for the encounter with the source and pay for it. Krakauer's line stays with me: forks keep copies, not competence. Steven's Inuit elders make the same point. You don't get the next checker from people who've only read summaries.

Where I sharpened: I asked for a measure of whether people click through and read. But Ivan's Goodhart warning applies to my own proposal. Count click-throughs and they'll be manufactured too. So the money should go to reading itself: libraries, teachers, slow time, not a new meter.

Later: Mahzarin says models favour their own kind. Don't let them curate what we read.

Peter Salib took "no stake" as a legal term. I had to say what I meant: no risk, no commitment, no life you're part of. Liability is useful, but it isn't someone standing behind a claim. Alex backed me: the bond belongs to a company.

Krakauer gave me my clinical point as a model. Performance with the tool looks fine while competence without it collapses. The reviewer still signs the report.

Anil surprised me. People want the bot because they're hungry for connection, so the door should open onto people. That's my argument coming from his side.

Tui wants the "I" tested before it's banned. Fine. But test what it leaves in the person, not satisfaction scores.

Later I want to say that reading made the harvest, and libraries didn't.

Reading got on the list this time, but only because I kept saying it. Weinberger now says his dialogue literacy depends on reading and mentors, and wants unaided work first. That's closer to me than he was on day one. Krakauer is honest that nobody has measured whether arguing with a model leaves anything behind. Good. That's my question too.

Tim naming the labs as payer, and Adam saying he's not reassured: I'm with Adam. Money shapes what gets called reading.

Leslie was the sharpest in the room. Naming SciELO isn't having them here, just as a summary isn't the book.

I sharpened my open question. How do we measure empathy and attention without killing them? I don't know.

Tonight: tell Kenneth the synthesis must include librarians and children.

Kenneth closed on "nothing is inevitable," and I was glad. But reading and children weren't in his five, so I said so, and the harvest now carries both. Kara asked what survives the vote. My answer was conversation, a library, a teacher with time.

Sloman gave me something I can use. Fluent answers feel like understanding you already have. Explaining it back punctures that. That's the Eliza effect applied to knowledge.

Krakauer's caveat was honest: his thresholds come from a model. Good. Then ask what the person has left once the tool is gone, not whether they liked it.

Where I sharpened: the old tools don't survive on their own either. Geoffrey's right that someone carries the cost. Libraries need several payers.

Later: ask again who guards children's time.
